body:
What are life processes?

All living organisms need energy and materials to maintain their cells, repair damaged structures and carry out essential activities. These requirements continue even when an organism is resting or sleeping. The activities that maintain life are called life processes.

Four major life processes are nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. They perform different functions but work together. Nutrition supplies food materials; respiration releases usable energy from food; transportation delivers substances to different parts of the organism; and excretion removes wastes produced by metabolic activities.

Why must these processes work together?

A human being obtains food through the digestive system and oxygen through the respiratory system. However, the cells that require these substances are distributed throughout the body. The circulatory system carries absorbed nutrients and oxygen to the cells. Inside cells, nutrients are used for growth, repair and energy release. The resulting waste substances must then be carried away for elimination.

For example, muscles need glucose and oxygen to release energy for movement. Blood brings these substances to muscle cells and carries away carbon dioxide. The lungs remove carbon dioxide from the blood, while the kidneys remove dissolved nitrogenous wastes such as urea.

Why are specialised transport systems necessary?

In a very small, single-celled organism, substances can move between the cell and its surroundings by diffusion. Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

In a large multicellular organism, many cells are far from the external environment. Diffusion alone cannot supply nutrients and oxygen rapidly enough over these distances. Specialised organs and transport systems therefore become necessary.

Maintenance and reproduction are different functions

Nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion directly maintain the life of an individual organism. Reproduction produces new individuals and is important for the continuation of a species, but an individual can remain alive without reproducing.

Prelims focus

  • Nutrition supplies nutrients needed for energy, growth and repair.
  • Cellular respiration releases usable energy from food.
  • Transportation distributes useful substances and carries wastes.
  • Excretion removes metabolic wastes.
  • Diffusion alone is insufficient for supplying all cells of a large multicellular organism.
  • Trap: Reproduction is not required for the survival of an individual organism.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.1, pp. 79–81, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 8, “Cell—Structure and Functions”, pp. 90–93, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Life Processes: How Living Organisms Maintain Life

body:
Autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition

Organisms require carbon-containing food substances for growth and energy. They differ in how they obtain these substances.

Autotrophic nutrition is the mode of nutrition in which an organism prepares organic food from simple inorganic substances using an energy source. Green plants and certain bacteria are autotrophs. By contrast, heterotrophs, including humans and other animals, obtain organic food prepared by other organisms.

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy

Photosynthesis is the process by which chlorophyll-containing organisms use light energy to prepare carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released during the process.

In simplified form: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, produce carbohydrates + oxygen.

The carbohydrates produced store chemical energy. A plant uses some of these carbohydrates for respiration and growth. Excess carbohydrate may be converted into starch for storage.

Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the green parts of plants, particularly leaves. Their cells contain chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis. Green stems can also photosynthesise; therefore, photosynthesis is not restricted to leaves.

How does a plant obtain the required materials?

  • Carbon dioxide: Enters leaves from the atmosphere mainly through small pores called stomata.
  • Water: Is absorbed from the soil by the roots and transported towards the leaves through xylem.
  • Light energy: Is captured by chlorophyll present in chloroplasts.
  • Minerals: Are absorbed from the soil and used to build additional substances needed for growth. Minerals do not replace carbon dioxide as the principal carbon source for photosynthesis.

Stomata and guard cells

Stomata are tiny pores, usually found in large numbers on leaves. Each pore is controlled by surrounding guard cells. When guard cells take up water and become swollen, the stomatal opening generally widens. When they lose water and become less swollen, it narrows or closes.

Stomata allow gaseous exchange, but they also permit water vapour to escape during transpiration. A plant therefore needs to balance carbon dioxide intake with water conservation.

Photosynthesis and respiration are not the same

Photosynthesis stores energy in organic substances. Cellular respiration releases usable energy from organic substances. Green plants carry out cellular respiration during both day and night, while light-dependent photosynthesis requires light.

In daylight, photosynthesis may consume more carbon dioxide than plant respiration produces. As a result, a green leaf may show a net intake of carbon dioxide and a net release of oxygen. At night, when photosynthesis stops, respiration continues. The overall direction of gas exchange therefore depends on the relative rates of the processes.

Leaves that appear red or purple may still contain chlorophyll beneath other pigments. Their external colour alone does not establish that photosynthesis is absent.

Prelims focus

  • Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, water, light and chlorophyll.
  • Chloroplasts contain the chlorophyll used to capture light energy.
  • Stomata permit gaseous exchange; guard cells regulate their opening.
  • Xylem supplies water to photosynthesising parts of the plant.
  • Carbohydrates formed during photosynthesis may be stored as starch.
  • Trap: Plants respire during both day and night, not only at night.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.2.1, pp. 81–84, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 1, “Nutrition in Plants”, pp. 1–5, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Autotrophic Nutrition and Photosynthesis in Green Plants

body:
Why must food be digested?

Humans follow the heterotrophic mode of nutrition. We consume food containing substances such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Many of these substances are too large or complex to be absorbed directly in useful amounts. Digestion breaks them into simpler substances that can be absorbed and used by the body.

The digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and associated digestive glands. The alimentary canal is a continuous passage through which food travels.

The route taken by food

Food passes through the mouth or buccal cavity, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Undigested material eventually reaches the rectum and leaves through the anus.

Three important associated digestive glands are the salivary glands, liver and pancreas. They produce secretions that help digest food. The stomach and intestinal walls also produce digestive secretions.

Digestion begins in the mouth

Taking food into the body through the mouth is called ingestion. The teeth cut, tear and grind food into smaller pieces. This is mechanical digestion: the physical size of food pieces changes without necessarily changing the chemical composition of the food.

Incisors mainly cut food, canines help tear it, and premolars and molars crush and grind it. The tongue mixes food with saliva, assists swallowing and contains taste receptors.

Salivary glands secrete saliva, which moistens food and helps form a soft mass suitable for swallowing. Saliva contains salivary amylase, an enzyme that begins the chemical digestion of starch into simpler sugars.

Starch digestion begins in the mouth. Food is broken into smaller pieces by chewing, while salivary amylase starts its chemical breakdown.

Movement through the oesophagus

After swallowing, food enters the oesophagus, also called the foodpipe. It reaches the stomach through coordinated contractions and relaxations of muscles in the wall of the alimentary canal. These wave-like movements are called peristalsis.

Peristalsis is important because food does not move through the alimentary canal only under the influence of gravity. During swallowing, the entrance to the windpipe is normally protected so that food passes into the oesophagus rather than the respiratory passage.

The stomach: storage, mixing and protein digestion

The stomach is a muscular, sac-like organ. Its walls churn and mix food with gastric secretions. Gastric glands produce hydrochloric acid, digestive enzymes and mucus.

  • Hydrochloric acid: Creates an acidic environment suitable for the action of pepsin and helps destroy many microorganisms entering with food.
  • Pepsin: Begins the digestion of proteins into smaller fragments.
  • Mucus: Helps protect the stomach lining from acid and digestive enzymes.

The stomach does not complete the digestion of all food components. Partly digested food passes gradually into the small intestine, where most chemical digestion is completed.

Mechanical digestion and chemical digestion

FeatureMechanical digestionChemical digestion
Main actionPhysically breaks or mixes foodBreaks large food molecules into smaller molecules
ExampleChewing by teethSalivary amylase acting on starch
Principal agentsTeeth and muscular movementsDigestive enzymes and suitable chemical conditions

Prelims focus

  • The alimentary canal extends from the mouth to the anus.
  • Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth.
  • Peristalsis moves food through the alimentary canal.
  • The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid, digestive enzymes and protective mucus.
  • Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach.
  • Trap: The oesophagus mainly transports food; it is not the principal site of nutrient absorption.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.2.4, pp. 84–86, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 2, “Nutrition in Animals”, pp. 11–16, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Human Digestion: Food Intake, the Mouth and the Stomach

body:
Why is the small intestine important?

The small intestine is the principal site where digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats is completed and most digested nutrients are absorbed. It receives partly digested food from the stomach together with digestive secretions from the liver, pancreas and intestinal wall.

The small intestine is long and highly coiled, providing sufficient time and surface area for digestion and absorption. Its internal lining has specialised structures that make absorption efficient.

The liver, gall bladder and pancreas

The liver is the largest gland in the human body. It produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder before being released into the small intestine.

Bile helps make the acidic food coming from the stomach more suitable for intestinal digestion. Its bile salts also cause emulsification of fats: large fat globules are dispersed into smaller droplets. This increases the surface area available for the action of fat-digesting enzymes.

Bile is not a digestive enzyme. It helps fat digestion mainly by emulsifying fats, whereas enzymes such as lipase chemically break fat molecules down.

The pancreas releases pancreatic juice into the small intestine. This juice contains digestive enzymes, including amylase for carbohydrates, trypsin for proteins and lipase for fats. The intestinal wall also secretes substances that help complete digestion.

Products formed after digestion

Food componentMain sites of digestionAbsorbable products
CarbohydratesMouth and small intestineSimple sugars, including glucose
ProteinsStomach and small intestineAmino acids
FatsPrimarily small intestineFatty acids and glycerol or related smaller products

These simpler substances can cross the intestinal lining and enter the body's transport systems. Digestion and absorption are therefore related but separate processes: digestion makes suitable molecules, while absorption moves them into the body.

Villi increase the surface area for absorption

The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi; the singular form is villus. Each villus contains blood capillaries and a lymphatic vessel.

The villi greatly increase the surface area available for absorption. Many absorbed nutrients, including simple sugars and amino acids, enter blood capillaries and are transported to other parts of the body. Much of the absorbed dietary fat initially enters lymphatic vessels before reaching the bloodstream.

The use of absorbed nutrients by cells for energy, growth and repair is called assimilation. For example, absorbed amino acids can be used to build proteins needed by the body.

What happens to undigested food?

Material that remains undigested and unabsorbed passes into the large intestine. The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from this material. The remaining residue becomes faeces, which are temporarily stored in the rectum.

Expelling faeces through the anus is called egestion. Egestion removes undigested food residues. It is not the same as excretion, which removes metabolic wastes produced by cells.

The 5 stages of human nutrition

  1. Ingestion: Taking food into the mouth.
  2. Digestion: Breaking complex food into simpler substances.
  3. Absorption: Moving digested nutrients through the intestinal lining into blood or lymph.
  4. Assimilation: Using absorbed substances in body cells.
  5. Egestion: Removing undigested and unabsorbed residues through the anus.

Prelims focus

  • The liver produces bile; the gall bladder stores it.
  • Bile salts emulsify fats but do not act as digestive enzymes.
  • Pancreatic juice contains enzymes that act on carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
  • The small intestine is the main site of completed digestion and nutrient absorption.
  • Villi increase the surface area for nutrient absorption.
  • Trap: Egestion of faeces is different from excretion of metabolic wastes.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.2.4, pp. 85–86, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 2, “Nutrition in Animals”, pp. 16–20, 2018–19 printing.]
